frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria uses pipeline and LNG supplies to deepen leverage with Europe, while European buyers seek diversification and tighter contractual terms.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability along the southern borders strains surveillance and infrastructure protection while competing foreign security relationships expand across the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies and lenders retain substantial influence over production, financing, and technology despite Luanda's efforts to increase national participation.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: US, European, and Chinese interests are competing for influence over the rail route and adjacent critical-minerals supply chains, limiting Angola's room to maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil export corridor is vulnerable to political disputes, border closures, and shifting regional alliances, putting infrastructure revenues at risk.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens transport links and encourages deeper reliance on foreign security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers relationship
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and marketing autonomy, but remains exposed to De Beers' global sales network and changing diamond demand.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals financing
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and battery-mineral projects could reduce diamond dependence, though foreign capital and infrastructure requirements may dilute state control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state and local participation in gold production, creating friction with foreign operators and increasing regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Insecurity around mining zones
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and contested territory threaten mines, roads, and artisanal production, while expanded Russian security ties add geopolitical exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border destabilization continue to constrain border trade and national security autonomy. Regional tensions also complicate Burundi's access to external transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mining and Export Networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold and prospective nickel development attract foreign capital, but weak oversight and informal export channels limit the state's ability to capture full resource value. Dependence on donors and foreign contractors further narrows policy space.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, telecommunications, and tourism remain heavily dependent on foreign investment and external markets. This creates exposure to changing European, Chinese, and transatlantic commercial priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Protection
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing places pressure on Cabo Verde's fisheries and enforcement capacity. The country relies on international partnerships and imported fuel and food to sustain maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to weaken state control over roads, farms, and commercial activity. Security operations and informal taxation raise costs for infrastructure and resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure and Extractives
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked construction and financing remain important to major transport projects, while oil, timber, and mining supply chains involve substantial foreign commercial influence. The state retains formal ownership but captures uneven value amid governance and transparency concerns.

highlights: State Authority Beyond Bangui Remains Limited

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection and counterinsurgency, while mining access and commercial concessions form part of the broader relationship. This limits independent oversight of gold and diamond production.

frictionVectors.title: Armed Groups and Fragile Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups continue to contest territory and transport routes outside the capital, especially near border zones. Weak logistics and dependence on foreign security partners prevent the government from exercising consistent control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Refugee Crisis
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan is driving refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border insecurity in eastern Chad. The crisis strains state capacity and increases reliance on foreign humanitarian and security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Dominated Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Oil production and the pipeline corridor through Cameroon remain dependent on foreign operators, finance, and technical expertise. Although hydrocarbons are the state's main strategic asset, revenue control and local development remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial reach and sustaining a persistent sovereignty dispute. The issue also affects migration management and access to surrounding maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, imported fuel, and external development finance. Limited state capacity constrains independent management of fisheries, ports, and potential offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains deeply integrated with Chinese-led refining, financing, and infrastructure networks. Kinshasa is seeking better terms and more local processing but still has limited leverage over the broader value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Linked Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and alleged external support continues to threaten territorial control, mining zones, and transport corridors in eastern Congo. Regional diplomacy and international pressure have not yet produced a durable security settlement.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and foreign-exchange earnings remain heavily dependent on offshore oil production, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and foreign operators. Diversification and transparent management of petroleum income remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects provide essential connectivity but increase dependence on external contractors and creditors. The government retains political control, while domestic value capture remains constrained.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Pricing and Foreign Processing
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening farmer incomes and domestic processing, but global traders and overseas manufacturers still capture much of the cocoa value chain. Climate stress and volatile prices add pressure to national control over export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion and transport links are attracting Gulf, European, Chinese, and regional investment. The country must balance this competition while preventing Sahel insecurity from disrupting northern corridors and critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities from the United States, China, France, Japan, and others, generating revenue and diplomatic leverage but narrowing strategic autonomy. Rivalry among these powers raises the risks surrounding national infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Ethiopian Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and logistics corridors are central to Ethiopia's trade, while Chinese financing and operators remain influential. Debt exposure and dependence on a single major hinterland market limit the government's room to manage infrastructure on fully sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF, Gulf, and other external financing remain important to Egypt's balance of payments. Privatization and foreign investment demands create pressure around state control of ports, utilities, and logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam dispute continues to frame Egypt's water security and regional diplomacy. Cairo is expanding partnerships and diplomatic pressure while avoiding a direct military confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited economic diversification weaken sovereign revenue and bargaining power. International energy firms retain influence over technology, investment, and future gas development.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Malabo and Bata remain exposed to competition among foreign maritime, construction, and security actors in the Gulf of Guinea. Infrastructure partnerships can expand state capacity but also deepen opaque external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract attention from Gulf, Western, and regional powers. Asmara seeks to monetize access while preserving strict control over ports and security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral projects provide foreign exchange but leave the economy dependent on a narrow group of external operators and commodity markets. Sanctions risk and limited transparency constrain broader investment.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Economic Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South Africa for trade, transport, energy links, and investment. This provides stability but limits independent bargaining power over infrastructure and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Political Legitimacy and Aid
frictionVectors.details: Governance concerns can affect access to concessional finance, donor support, and foreign investment. External partners balance pressure for reform against the need to preserve regional stability.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Escalation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over power generation and regional water diplomacy but continues to provoke acute Egyptian and Sudanese concerns. Disagreement over filling, operations, and data sharing remains unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western actors compete for influence over transport, energy, telecoms, and agricultural assets. Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain Addis Ababa's ability to dictate terms independently.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive chains
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture in oil, manganese, and timber, but production, logistics, and financing remain heavily dependent on foreign firms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port infrastructure remain vulnerable to external commercial influence, limiting Libreville's ability to fully control mineral flows.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on imported fuel, donor-backed infrastructure, and regional electricity arrangements, leaving strategic sectors exposed to external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and fisheries vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders dominate key agricultural and fishing value chains, while maritime enforcement remains insufficient to secure national resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions narrow policy space, although macroeconomic stabilization is improving the government's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold mining and lithium competition
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems and undermine state control, while foreign interest in lithium and gold tests Accra's ability to secure local processing and fair fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite and iron-ore enclave economics
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and regional investors compete for access to bauxite and Simandou, while Guinea still struggles to convert mineral exports into broad-based domestic industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Transition legitimacy and infrastructure control
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government uses mining and corridor projects to bolster legitimacy, but political uncertainty and opaque contracting increase sovereign and operational risk.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of cashew trade
frictionVectors.details: Exporters and external buyers capture much of the cashew value chain, leaving the state exposed to price shocks and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics, and security networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested political authority complicate control of the port and maritime space, creating openings for trafficking networks and external security influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and dependence on multilateral financing constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners compete for influence through transport, energy, and logistics projects.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in ports, rail, and logistics remains politically sensitive because it can affect strategic access to Kenya's main trade gateway.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on Pretoria for infrastructure, market access, and project financing.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned textile production and reliance on imported energy expose Lesotho to external market decisions and supply disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other concessions generate badly needed revenue but leave the state exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over local content.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign control or financing of mining-linked railways and port facilities can limit Liberia's ability to capture value beyond royalties and concession fees.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Institution Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security centers contest control of oil revenues, export terminals, and national institutions, making resource policy highly vulnerable to coercion.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military, political, and commercial actors support rival Libyan factions and seek influence over energy infrastructure, migration routes, and reconstruction contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining projects are dominated by foreign capital, creating tensions over fiscal returns, environmental costs, and domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on imported fuel weaken Madagascar's bargaining position with external financiers and infrastructure operators.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and donor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor financing limit room for independent spending and industrial policy. Fiscal consolidation is intensifying pressure on subsidies and public services.

frictionVectors.title: Input and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fertilizer, fuel, and electricity exposes Malawi to external price shocks. Chinese and other foreign-backed infrastructure provides connectivity but does not eliminate underlying supply-chain dependence.

highlights: Junta tightens control over strategic minerals

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking a larger share of gold revenues and greater control over foreign mining operators, creating recurring disputes over permits, taxes, and operating conditions. Industrial mining remains heavily dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has reduced Western influence but increased exposure to opaque security-for-resource arrangements. Ongoing conflict and strained ties with regional and Western institutions continue to threaten transport and mining corridors.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers Mauritania new export revenue and diplomatic weight, but foreign operators, financing, and cross-border infrastructure retain substantial control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and coastal corridor pressure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore logistics and fisheries depend on vulnerable export infrastructure and external markets. Competition over maritime resources, licensing, and local employment remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over basing, security, and the future of Diego Garcia. Any settlement must balance decolonization objectives with major-power military interests.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and blue-economy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control, but its finance, tourism, and maritime sectors are highly exposed to external regulation and global capital cycles. Competition over seabed resources and ocean governance is likely to grow.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the core fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, renewables, and infrastructure in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's territorial strategy and a source of friction with Algeria and the Polisario Front. Foreign investment and trade agreements continue to face legal and diplomatic scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is attracting European, Gulf, Chinese, and US-linked investment into ports, automotive production, renewables, and green hydrogen. This diversification strengthens national capacity while creating competing external dependencies around technology, finance, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led LNG projects remain central to Mozambique’s fiscal and export strategy, but insurgency continues to limit sovereign control over the gas corridor. Any sustained restart depends on external security support and private operators.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Coal, graphite and logistics projects rely heavily on foreign capital and concession agreements. Weak local linkages and public-debt pressures constrain the state’s bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries could transform Namibia’s fiscal position, but development is led by international energy companies. The government faces pressure to secure stronger local-content, taxation and environmental provisions.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, technology and export markets. Water scarcity and unresolved benefit-sharing concerns could generate domestic resistance to externally driven infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger’s crude exports depend on cross-border infrastructure and political access through neighboring states, leaving revenue vulnerable to diplomatic disputes and border closures. The state’s stronger negotiating posture has not removed these logistical constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating relations with Western firms while expanding security ties with Russia and other non-Western partners. This diversification increases autonomy but also raises uncertainty over mining investment, sanctions and operational security.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Niger Delta Control
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage and illegal refining continue to weaken state capture of petroleum revenues. International operators remain important, while local communities demand greater ownership and compensation.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Refinery Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Expanded domestic refining and gas investment could reduce dependence on imported fuel, but financing, regulation and unreliable infrastructure remain significant obstacles. Foreign capital and technology are still essential to scaling the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Linkages
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s regional security posture and mineral-trading networks face persistent international scrutiny over alleged links to conflict resources from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Diplomatic pressure could affect export access and relations with Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong domestic state capacity supports strategic control over infrastructure and mining policy, but the economy remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance and external investors. Shifts in donor policy could narrow Kigali’s room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Exploration Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain dependent on foreign operators and financing, while limited state capacity constrains São Tomé and Príncipe's leverage over offshore licensing.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's location near Gulf of Guinea shipping routes attracts external security partnerships, but weak maritime surveillance leaves fisheries and offshore assets vulnerable.

highlights: Oil and gas sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Reset
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers fiscal upside, but disputes over contract terms, local content, and foreign operators will test Dakar's ability to convert resources into durable sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Fisheries Stress
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and foreign fishing agreements continue to strain coastal communities, with enforcement and transparency central to Senegal's resource-security agenda.

highlights: Small-state balancing in the Indian Ocean

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Access to Maritime Assets
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances Indian, Chinese, European, and other external interests around ports, maritime surveillance, and fisheries while seeking to preserve policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Climate Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism concentration, climate vulnerability, and dependence on external climate finance limit the state's room to manage its ocean resources without outside conditions.

highlights: Mining drives growth, bargaining power remains limited

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining remains central to exports and public revenue, leaving Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and concerns over contract fairness, local processing, and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: External investors seek influence over ports, roads, energy, and mining logistics, creating opportunities for infrastructure development but also long-term strategic and fiscal liabilities.

highlights: Ports and offshore resources are strategic prizes

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, China, and other actors compete for access to Somali ports and maritime infrastructure, often through arrangements that outpace federal-state coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Governance and Security
frictionVectors.details: Potential offshore hydrocarbons, fisheries, and other resources remain constrained by al-Shabaab violence, weak institutions, and disputes over authority between Mogadishu and federal member states.

highlights: Power and ports remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL AND BENEFICIATION
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare minerals while remaining dependent on foreign capital, technology, and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND LOGISTICS CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port bottlenecks continue to limit sovereign control over industrial output and mineral exports, creating openings for external infrastructure and financing partners.

highlights: Peace and pipeline security are fragile

frictionVectors.title: OIL REVENUE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal system depends heavily on oil exports routed through Sudan, leaving production, revenue flows, and bargaining power vulnerable to external operators and transit disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: TRANSITIONAL SECURITY FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and armed mobilization continue to threaten transport corridors, oil infrastructure, and humanitarian access, weakening state control over strategic assets.

highlights: Gold and corridors attract competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: GOLD ECONOMY AND EXTERNAL PATRONS
frictionVectors.details: Control of gold-producing areas and export channels is tied to rival military networks and foreign commercial or security interests, diverting value away from formal state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, PIPELINES, AND HUMANITARIAN CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: The conflict threatens Sudan's Red Sea infrastructure and oil-transit routes while external actors compete for access, logistics influence, and political leverage.

highlights: Ports and LNG are strategic leverage points

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT AND CONTRACT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing offshore gas development while negotiating fiscal terms, local content, and infrastructure commitments with international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and neighboring transport corridors are drawing competing Chinese, Gulf, and Western commercial interest, creating leverage but also exposing Tanzania to strategic dependency.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway
Security pressures reach the northern frontier

frictionVectors.title: PORT-LED EXTERNAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and logistics economy rely on foreign shipping, finance, and regional transit demand, giving outside commercial actors influence over a critical national asset.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel increase pressure on northern transport routes and security infrastructure, encouraging deeper external security involvement.

highlights: EU Leverage Over Migration and Energy

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic criticism remains strong over perceived outsourcing of border control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and external financing while recurring phosphate-sector disruptions limit export earnings and fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed East African Crude Oil Pipeline strengthens Uganda's route to monetizing oil but faces Western political, legal, and financing pressure over environmental and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked capital is increasingly important in energy, transport, and extractive projects, raising concerns about long-term revenue-sharing and operating-control terms.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Addition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and transparency in copper deals, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Threaten Mining Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower deficits and drought-driven electricity shortages constrain copper output and increase dependence on regional power imports and emergency infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Dominance in Lithium and Mining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese companies remain central to lithium and other mineral investment, providing processing capacity but limiting Zimbabwe's bargaining power over technology, financing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions, and restricted access to international finance weaken the state's ability to capture predictable mineral revenues or fund domestic infrastructure.
